stem: The major economic reforms in India were introduced in the year:
solution: The major economic reforms in India — the New Economic Policy of Liberalisation, Privatisation, and Globalisation (LPG) — were introduced in 1991. These reforms marked a fundamental change in India's economic policy, moving away from the earlier model of heavy government control and a closed, inward-looking economy toward a more open, market-oriented economy. They were prompted by a severe economic crisis that India faced in 1991. Understanding that the reforms began in 1991 is a key prelims point. India's major economic reforms (LPG) were introduced in 1991.

stem: The economic reforms of 1991 were triggered by a severe economic __________ that India was facing.
solution: The economic reforms of 1991 were triggered by a severe economic crisis — in particular, a grave balance-of-payments (foreign-exchange) crisis. By 1991, India's foreign-exchange reserves had fallen so low that they were barely enough to pay for even a couple of weeks of imports; the country was on the verge of defaulting on its international payments; it faced a large fiscal deficit and mounting debt; and inflation was high. To deal with this crisis (and as a condition of the emergency loans it took from the IMF and World Bank), India was forced to change its economic policies and undertake the reforms. Understanding that a crisis (foreign-exchange/balance-of-payments) triggered the 1991 reforms is a key prelims point. The 1991 reforms were triggered by a severe economic crisis, especially a balance-of-payments (foreign-exchange) crisis.

stem: The reforms of 1991 are often summed up by the abbreviation 'LPG', which stands for Liberalisation, Privatisation, and:
solution: The reforms of 1991 are often summed up by the abbreviation 'LPG', standing for Liberalisation, Privatisation, and Globalisation — the three main components/pillars of the New Economic Policy: (1) Liberalisation — freeing the economy from many government controls and regulations; (2) Privatisation — giving a greater role to the private sector (and reducing the role of the public sector); and (3) Globalisation — integrating the Indian economy with the world economy (through trade and investment). Understanding what LPG stands for is a key prelims point. 'LPG' stands for Liberalisation, Privatisation, and Globalisation.

stem: Liberalisation refers to:
options: the freeing/removal of unnecessary government controls, restrictions, and regulations on the economy (like licensing)
solution: Liberalisation refers to the freeing (liberating) of the economy from many of the government's controls, restrictions, and regulations — making the economy freer and more market-oriented. It included measures such as: the abolition of industrial licensing (ending the 'License Raj') for most industries; the removal of restrictions on the private sector; the easing of controls on foreign trade and investment; and reforms of the financial sector, tax system, and so on. The idea was that, freed from excessive controls, businesses could operate more freely and efficiently, and market forces could work better. Understanding liberalisation (freeing the economy from controls) is a key prelims point. Liberalisation is the freeing of the economy from unnecessary government controls, restrictions, and regulations.

stem: Privatisation refers to:
options: increasing the role of the public sector
reducing the role of the public sector and giving a greater role to the private sector (e.g., selling government stakes in public enterprises)
solution: Privatisation refers to reducing the role of the public sector (government-owned enterprises) and giving a greater role to the private sector in the economy. It can take forms such as: 'disinvestment' — the government selling off part (or all) of its shares/ownership in public-sector enterprises (to private buyers/the public); the outright transfer of ownership and management of public enterprises to private hands; and opening up sectors that were reserved for the public sector to private companies. The aim was to improve efficiency (private enterprises being seen as more efficient than the loss-making public units) and to raise resources. Understanding privatisation (shrinking the public sector, expanding the private sector) is a key prelims point. Privatisation is reducing the role of the public sector and giving a greater role to the private sector.

stem: Globalisation refers to:
options: isolating the economy from the world
integrating the country's economy with the world economy (through freer trade, investment, and flows of technology, capital, and people)
producing only for the domestic market
solution: Globalisation refers to the integration of a country's economy with the economies of the rest of the world — making the national economy more open to, and interconnected with, the global economy. It involves the freer flow of goods and services (trade), capital and investment (like foreign investment), technology, and even people, across national borders. For India, globalisation (from 1991) meant opening up the economy to foreign trade and investment, reducing barriers (like tariffs and restrictions), and linking Indian producers and markets with the world. The aim was to make the economy more competitive and to reap the benefits of participating in the global economy. Understanding globalisation (integrating with the world economy) is a key prelims point. Globalisation is the integration of the country's economy with the world economy, through freer trade, investment, and flows of technology and capital.

stem: A key measure of liberalisation in the industrial sector was the __________ of industrial licensing for most industries.
solution: A key measure of liberalisation in the industrial sector was the abolition (removal) of industrial licensing for most industries — that is, ending the requirement that businesses obtain a government licence to start, expand, or change an industry (the dismantling of the 'License Raj'). After 1991, industrial licensing was abolished for almost all industries (only a small number of industries — related to security, strategic, or environmental/social concerns — still required a licence). This freed entrepreneurs to set up and expand industries according to market opportunities, without seeking government permission. Understanding the abolition of industrial licensing is a key prelims point. A key liberalisation measure was the abolition of industrial licensing for most industries.

stem: Under the reforms, the number of industries reserved exclusively for the public sector was:
options: greatly reduced (to only a few strategic ones)
solution: Under the reforms of 1991, the number of industries reserved exclusively for the public sector was greatly reduced. Earlier (under IPR 1956), a large number of key industries were reserved only for the state (public sector); after the reforms, this list was cut down drastically, so that only a very few industries (of strategic importance — such as atomic energy, and railways) remained reserved for the public sector, while the rest were opened up to the private sector. This reflected the shift toward a greater role for private enterprise (privatisation) and away from the dominance of the public sector. Understanding the reduction of public-sector reservation is a prelims point. The reforms greatly reduced the number of industries reserved exclusively for the public sector (to only a few strategic ones).

stem: The sale of a part of the government's shareholding in a public-sector enterprise (to private investors or the public) is called:
solution: Disinvestment is the process by which the government sells off a part (or the whole) of its shareholding/ownership in a public-sector enterprise (PSE) — to private investors, financial institutions, or the general public. Disinvestment is a form/instrument of privatisation. The government undertakes disinvestment for reasons such as: to raise revenue/resources; to improve the efficiency of the enterprises (by bringing in private ownership, management, and discipline); and to reduce the government's burden of running (and financing) loss-making public units. Understanding disinvestment (selling government stakes in PSEs) is a prelims point. Disinvestment is the sale of a part of the government's shareholding in a public-sector enterprise.

stem: Globalisation measures included the reduction of tariffs (import duties) and the removal of many restrictions on __________.
solution: The globalisation measures of the reforms included steps to open up the economy to the world, such as: reducing tariffs (import duties/taxes) on imported goods; removing many quantitative restrictions and quotas on imports and exports; making the rupee convertible (allowing freer exchange of the currency for trade); and easing/removing restrictions on foreign investment — allowing foreign companies to invest in India (Foreign Direct Investment) and encouraging foreign capital and technology to flow in. In short, globalisation involved reducing the barriers to foreign trade and foreign investment, integrating India with the world economy. Understanding these globalisation measures (freeing trade and investment) is a prelims point. Globalisation measures reduced tariffs and removed many restrictions on foreign trade and foreign investment.

stem: The investment made by foreign companies/individuals in the businesses of another country (setting up or acquiring enterprises) is called:
solution: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is the investment made by foreign companies or individuals directly into the businesses/enterprises of another country — for example, by setting up new factories/companies, or by acquiring a stake in existing companies, in that country. FDI is different from mere financial investment: it involves a lasting interest and often brings not just capital but also technology, management expertise, and access to global markets. The globalisation reforms encouraged FDI into India (by easing the restrictions on it), to bring in capital, technology, and jobs. Understanding FDI (foreign investment in businesses) is a prelims point. Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is the investment by foreign firms/individuals directly in the businesses of another country.

stem: The international organisation (set up in 1995) that deals with the rules of trade between nations and promotes free/liberalised international trade is the:
solution: The World Trade Organization (WTO) is the international organisation (established in 1995, as the successor to the earlier GATT — the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade) that deals with the rules of trade between nations. Its main aim is to promote and facilitate free, fair, and liberalised international trade — by getting member countries to reduce trade barriers (tariffs and restrictions), and by providing a framework of trade rules and a mechanism to settle trade disputes. India is a member of the WTO. As part of globalisation, India's membership of the WTO committed it to opening up its trade. Understanding the WTO (rules of international trade) is a prelims point. The World Trade Organization (WTO), set up in 1995, deals with the rules of trade between nations and promotes free international trade.

stem: The service sector (especially IT — information technology and software, and business services) grew very rapidly in India after the reforms, making it a major contributor to:
options: India's growth and exports (and a source of employment)
solution: After the reforms, the service sector — especially the information technology (IT) and software industry, and IT-enabled/business services (like call centres, BPO — Business Process Outsourcing) — grew very rapidly in India, and it became a major contributor to India's economic growth and to its exports (India became a leading global exporter of software and IT services), as well as a significant source of (skilled) employment. The rise of the IT/services sector is one of the notable features of India's post-reform economy (with cities like Bangalore/Bengaluru and Hyderabad becoming IT hubs). Understanding the rapid growth of the service/IT sector after the reforms is a prelims point. After the reforms, the service sector (especially IT/software) grew rapidly, becoming a major contributor to India's growth and exports.

stem: A major POSITIVE effect (appraisal) of the reforms was that India's rate of economic __________ increased.
solution: A major positive effect of the reforms was that India's rate of economic growth (GDP growth) increased — the economy grew faster after the reforms than it had during the earlier decades of the slow 'Hindu rate of growth'. Post-1991, India moved onto a higher growth path (with growth accelerating, especially from the 2000s, to among the fastest in the world). Along with faster growth, the reforms also brought other gains: a big increase in foreign-exchange reserves (ending the crisis), a boom in the service/IT sector, more foreign investment, a greater availability and variety of goods, and India's emergence as a major, more confident participant in the global economy. Understanding that the reforms raised India's growth rate is a key prelims point. A major positive effect of the reforms was an increase in India's rate of economic (GDP) growth.

stem: A major CRITICISM of the reforms (an 'appraisal' point) is that the growth was not accompanied by enough growth of __________, so unemployment remained a problem ('jobless growth').
solution: A major criticism of the reforms is that the faster economic growth was NOT accompanied by a corresponding growth of employment (jobs) — a phenomenon called 'jobless growth'. That is, output/GDP grew rapidly, but the number of jobs created did not grow fast enough to absorb the growing labour force, so unemployment (and underemployment) remained a serious problem, and the benefits of growth did not reach a large section of the people through jobs. (This was partly because much of the growth was in the capital-intensive and service sectors, which create fewer jobs per unit of output.) So 'jobless growth' is a key criticism in the appraisal of the reforms. Understanding the 'jobless growth' criticism is a prelims point. A major criticism of the reforms is 'jobless growth' — growth not accompanied by enough employment growth.

stem: Another criticism of the reforms is that they NEGLECTED the __________ sector, which grew slowly and where public investment was reduced.
solution: Another criticism of the reforms is that they neglected the agricultural sector. After the reforms, agriculture grew slowly (its growth rate fell), and the sector faced several problems: public investment in agriculture (in irrigation, infrastructure, research) was reduced; the removal of subsidies and the opening up to global competition increased the difficulties and costs for farmers; and there was inadequate support. Since a very large part of India's population still depends on agriculture, this neglect (and the resulting agrarian distress) was a serious shortcoming of the reforms. So the neglect of agriculture is a key criticism in the appraisal of the reforms. Understanding the neglect-of-agriculture criticism is a prelims point. A key criticism of the reforms is the neglect of agriculture, which grew slowly and saw reduced public investment.

stem: A further criticism is that the reforms increased __________ — the gap between the rich and the poor, and between developed and backward regions.
solution: A further criticism of the reforms is that they increased inequality (disparities) — widening the gap between the rich and the poor, and between the more developed and the more backward regions/states (and between sectors). The benefits of the reforms and of the faster growth were unevenly distributed: they tended to benefit more the already better-off sections (the skilled, the urban, the industrial/service sectors, and the more developed regions), while the poor, the rural areas, agriculture, and the backward regions benefited less (or were even hurt). So, although growth increased, the reforms are criticised for making the distribution of income and development more unequal. Understanding the rising-inequality criticism is a prelims point. A key criticism of the reforms is that they increased inequality — widening the gaps between rich and poor and between regions.

stem: The reforms brought a large increase in India's foreign-exchange reserves, which had the effect of:
options: ending the balance-of-payments crisis and giving the economy stability and confidence
solution: The reforms (with the boost to exports, foreign investment, and confidence) brought a large increase in India's foreign-exchange reserves — from the crisis level of 1991 (barely enough for a couple of weeks of imports) to comfortable and then very large reserves. This had the important positive effect of ending the balance-of-payments crisis that had triggered the reforms, and of giving the economy stability, security, and confidence (the country was no longer at risk of defaulting on its international payments, and it could comfortably finance its imports and withstand external shocks). Building up the foreign-exchange reserves was thus one of the clear successes of the reforms. Understanding this positive effect (rising forex reserves, ending the crisis) is a prelims point. The reforms greatly increased India's foreign-exchange reserves, ending the balance-of-payments crisis and giving stability and confidence.

stem: The NITI Aayog, which replaced the Planning Commission in 2015, reflects the changed role of the state in the economy — from a __________ role to more of an advisory/facilitating role.
solution: The NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India), which replaced the old Planning Commission in 2015, reflects the changed role of the state in the post-reform, more market-oriented economy: it marks a shift away from the earlier directing/controlling (command) role of the state (in which the Planning Commission drew up detailed, binding Five Year Plans and allocated resources in a centralised way) toward more of an advisory, facilitating, and coordinating role — the NITI Aayog acts as a think-tank that gives policy advice, promotes cooperative federalism (working with the states), and facilitates development, rather than commanding the economy. This reflects the reduced, more enabling role of the state after liberalisation. Understanding what the shift to NITI Aayog reflects is a prelims-relevant point. NITI Aayog (2015) replaced the Planning Commission, reflecting the state's shift from a directing/controlling role to an advisory/facilitating one.

stem: Assertion (A): The 1991 reforms increased India's rate of economic growth. Reason (R): By freeing the economy from excessive controls and opening it to competition, trade, and investment, the reforms improved efficiency and encouraged enterprise. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that the 1991 reforms increased India's rate of economic growth. And the reason is (R) that, by freeing the economy from the excessive controls of the earlier era (abolishing licensing, reducing restrictions) and by opening it up to competition, foreign trade, and investment, the reforms improved efficiency (as businesses had to compete and could operate more freely) and encouraged enterprise, investment, and the inflow of capital and technology — all of which spurred faster growth. So the freeing-up and opening-up of the economy (R) is exactly what raised the growth rate (A). Understanding this cause-effect is a prelims point. The reforms raised growth because freeing the economy from controls and opening it to competition, trade, and investment improved efficiency and enterprise.

stem: The Finance Minister who introduced the 1991 economic reforms (in the government of P.V. Narasimha Rao) was:
solution: Dr. Manmohan Singh was the Finance Minister (in the government of Prime Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao) who introduced and steered the landmark economic reforms of 1991 (the LPG reforms/New Economic Policy). An economist by training, Manmohan Singh is closely associated with these reforms that opened up and liberalised the Indian economy. (He later became the Prime Minister of India, 2004–2014.) Understanding that Manmohan Singh (as Finance Minister) introduced the 1991 reforms is a prelims point. Dr. Manmohan Singh, as Finance Minister under P.V. Narasimha Rao, introduced the 1991 economic reforms.

stem: One immediate cause of the 1991 crisis was a sharp rise in oil prices due to the:
solution: One immediate/triggering cause of the 1991 economic crisis was a sharp rise in international oil prices caused by the Gulf War (of 1990–91, following Iraq's invasion of Kuwait). Since India imports much of its oil, the spike in oil prices sharply increased India's import bill (worsening the balance of payments), and the Gulf crisis also cut off the remittances from Indian workers in the Gulf and disrupted trade. Coming on top of India's already weak finances (high fiscal deficit, mounting debt, low reserves), this oil shock helped push India into the foreign-exchange crisis of 1991. Understanding the Gulf War/oil-price shock as a cause of the crisis is a prelims point. A rise in oil prices due to the Gulf War (1990–91) was an immediate cause of the 1991 crisis.

stem: During the 1991 crisis, India's foreign-exchange reserves had fallen so low that they were barely enough to pay for about __________ of imports.
solution: During the 1991 crisis, India's foreign-exchange reserves had fallen so low that they were barely enough to pay for only about two weeks of imports (some accounts say a couple of weeks/a fortnight). This dangerously low level of reserves meant that India was on the very brink of being unable to pay for its essential imports and of defaulting on its international debt payments — a grave balance-of-payments crisis. This desperate situation is what forced India to seek emergency loans (from the IMF and World Bank) and to undertake the economic reforms. Understanding how low the reserves fell (about two weeks of imports) conveys the severity of the crisis — a prelims point. In 1991, India's forex reserves were barely enough for about two weeks of imports.

stem: To tide over the 1991 crisis, India borrowed emergency loans from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank, which required India to undertake __________ in return.
options: economic reforms (structural adjustment — liberalising and opening up the economy)
solution: To tide over the 1991 balance-of-payments crisis, India borrowed emergency loans from the International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the World Bank. In return for (as a condition of) these loans, these institutions required India to undertake economic reforms — a 'Structural Adjustment Programme' — that is, to liberalise, privatise, and open up (globalise) its economy (reduce controls, cut the fiscal deficit, open up to trade and investment, etc.). So the reforms were partly driven by these external conditions attached to the IMF/World Bank loans (as well as by India's own recognition of the need for change). Understanding that the IMF/World Bank loans required reforms (structural adjustment) is a prelims point. India's emergency IMF/World Bank loans in 1991 required it to undertake economic reforms (structural adjustment) — liberalising and opening up the economy.

stem: As part of the 1991 reforms, the Indian rupee was __________ (its external value was reduced), to make exports cheaper and correct the balance of payments.
solution: As part of the 1991 reforms (to address the balance-of-payments crisis), the Indian rupee was devalued — that is, its external value (exchange rate against foreign currencies) was deliberately reduced/lowered. Devaluation makes a country's exports cheaper (and more competitive) for foreigners and its imports more expensive — which helps to boost exports and curb imports, thereby helping to correct the balance-of-payments deficit and earn foreign exchange. (Along with devaluation, the exchange rate was later moved toward being market-determined, and the rupee was made convertible on the current account.) Understanding the devaluation of the rupee (in the 1991 reforms) is a prelims point. In 1991, the rupee was devalued (its value reduced) to make exports cheaper and help correct the balance of payments.

stem: The reform measures are broadly of two kinds: short-run 'stabilisation measures' (to correct the immediate crisis) and long-run '__________ reform measures' (to improve the economy's efficiency).
solution: The reform measures of 1991 were broadly of two kinds: (1) 'stabilisation measures' — short-run measures aimed at correcting the immediate weaknesses/crisis, i.e., controlling the balance-of-payments deficit and bringing inflation under control (getting the economy stable again); and (2) 'structural reform measures' — long-run measures aimed at improving the efficiency of the economy and increasing its international competitiveness, by removing the rigidities and controls in the various sectors (i.e., the liberalisation, privatisation, and globalisation measures that changed the basic structure/functioning of the economy). So stabilisation was the short-term fix, and structural reform the long-term transformation. Understanding the two kinds of reform measures (stabilisation and structural) is a prelims point. The reforms were of two kinds: short-run stabilisation measures and long-run structural reform measures.

stem: Under the reforms, the role of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) changed from a 'controller' of the financial sector to more of a __________.
solution: Under the financial-sector reforms, the role of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) changed from being a rigid 'controller' of the financial sector (tightly directing and controlling banks and financial institutions) to being more of a facilitator and regulator — setting the rules and overseeing the sector, while allowing the financial institutions more freedom to take their own decisions on many matters. As part of these reforms: private-sector banks (Indian and foreign) were allowed to open; the controls on banks were eased; foreign investment in banks was permitted; and institutions like SEBI were strengthened to regulate the capital market. So the RBI moved from micro-controlling to facilitating/regulating a freer financial sector. Understanding the RBI's changed role (controller → facilitator/regulator) is a prelims point. Under the reforms, the RBI's role changed from a controller to a facilitator/regulator of the financial sector.

stem: The reforms allowed foreign investors — 'Foreign Institutional Investors' (FIIs) like foreign banks and mutual funds — to invest in India's:
solution: The reforms opened up India's financial markets to Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) — foreign institutions such as merchant/investment banks, mutual funds, pension funds, and insurance companies — allowing them to invest in India's financial (stock/capital) markets (buying shares and bonds). This brought in foreign capital (portfolio investment) and helped develop and deepen India's capital markets. (This is a form of 'foreign portfolio/financial investment', distinct from FDI, which is direct investment in businesses.) The entry of FIIs was part of the globalisation/financial-sector reforms. Understanding that FIIs were allowed to invest in India's financial markets is a prelims point. The reforms allowed Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) to invest in India's financial (stock/capital) markets.

stem: As part of tax (fiscal) reforms, the rates of direct taxes (like income tax) were generally:
solution: As part of the tax (fiscal) reforms, the rates of direct taxes — such as personal income tax and corporate (company) tax — were generally reduced (lowered) from the very high levels of the earlier era. The reasoning was that: very high tax rates encouraged tax evasion (people hid income to avoid the high taxes); moderate/lower rates would encourage people to declare their income and pay their taxes honestly (improving compliance), and would boost savings, investment, and enterprise. So lowering the direct-tax rates was expected to actually increase tax revenue (by improving compliance) and to spur economic activity. (There were also reforms of indirect taxes — simplifying them, and later moving toward a unified Goods and Services Tax, GST.) Understanding the reduction of direct-tax rates is a prelims point. Tax reforms generally reduced the rates of direct taxes (like income tax) to improve compliance and encourage enterprise.

stem: The unified indirect tax introduced in India in 2017 (replacing many separate indirect taxes), as part of the continuing reforms, is the:
solution: The Goods and Services Tax (GST) is the unified, nationwide indirect tax introduced in India in 2017, replacing the many separate indirect taxes that had been levied by the central and state governments (like excise duty, service tax, VAT, etc.). GST is a single tax on the supply of goods and services across the country, aimed at creating a common national market, simplifying the tax system, removing the cascading (tax-on-tax) effect, and making the system more efficient and transparent. It represents a major continuation of the economic reforms (of the tax system). Understanding that GST (2017) is the unified indirect tax is a prelims-relevant point. The Goods and Services Tax (GST), introduced in 2017, is India's unified indirect tax, replacing many earlier separate indirect taxes.

stem: A striking feature of India's post-reform growth is that it has been led mainly by the __________ sector, rather than by manufacturing/industry.
solution: A striking feature of India's post-reform growth is that it has been led mainly by the service sector (services like IT/software, telecommunications, finance, trade, business services, etc.), rather than by the manufacturing/industrial sector. The services sector grew very fast and became the largest contributor to India's GDP and growth. This is considered somewhat unusual (and a matter of concern), because normally, in the course of development, an economy moves from agriculture to manufacturing and then to services — whereas India seemed to move from agriculture largely to services, with manufacturing/industry growing more slowly and not creating enough jobs. This service-led growth (and the lagging of manufacturing) is a notable point in the appraisal of the reforms. Understanding that India's growth has been service-led is a prelims point. India's post-reform growth has been led mainly by the service sector, rather than by manufacturing/industry.

stem: The process by which a company gets some of its work/services done by an outside agency (often in another country, to save costs) — a major source of jobs in India — is called:
solution: Outsourcing is the process by which a company gets some of its work or services done by an outside agency/company (rather than doing it in-house) — and often this outside agency is located in another country (to take advantage of lower costs and skilled labour). With globalisation and improvements in IT/communications, India became a major destination for outsourcing — especially the outsourcing of IT-enabled services and business processes (BPO — Business Process Outsourcing, like call centres, back-office work, data processing, etc.) by companies from developed countries. This brought in business, foreign exchange, and (skilled, especially English-speaking) jobs to India. Understanding outsourcing (and India as a hub for it) is a prelims-relevant point. Outsourcing is getting work/services done by an outside (often foreign) agency; India became a major hub for outsourcing (BPO), a source of jobs.

stem: India became a favoured destination for outsourcing (like call centres and BPOs) largely because of its:
options: large pool of low-cost, skilled, English-speaking workers
solution: India became a favoured (leading) destination for outsourcing — for IT-enabled services and business-process outsourcing (call centres, back-office operations, software work, etc.) — largely because of its large pool of low-cost, skilled, and English-speaking workers. Companies in developed countries (like the USA and UK) could get their work done in India at much lower cost, by educated Indian workers who could speak English and were skilled in IT and other services — combined with the time-zone difference (allowing round-the-clock work) and India's improving telecom/IT infrastructure. These advantages made India a global outsourcing hub, bringing jobs and foreign exchange. Understanding why India attracts outsourcing is a prelims-relevant point. India became a top outsourcing destination because of its large pool of low-cost, skilled, English-speaking workers.

stem: A concern about the effect of globalisation on small domestic producers/industries is that they:
options: face tough competition from cheaper imported goods and big multinational companies (which can drive some of them out of business)
solution: A concern about the effect of globalisation on small domestic producers and industries is that, with the opening up of the economy, they now face tough competition from cheaper imported goods (from abroad, including from countries like China) and from big, powerful multinational companies (MNCs) entering the Indian market. The small-scale and domestic producers (with fewer resources, older technology, and higher costs) often struggle to compete with these bigger, cheaper rivals — and some of them are driven out of business (leading to closures and job losses). So while globalisation gives consumers more choice and cheaper goods, it can hurt the small and vulnerable domestic producers who cannot withstand the competition. This is a key concern in the appraisal of globalisation. Understanding this concern (globalisation hurting small producers) is a prelims point. Globalisation exposes small domestic producers to tough competition from cheap imports and big multinationals, which can drive some out of business.

stem: As a member of the WTO, India (like other developing countries) has argued that the developed countries have NOT fully honoured their commitments — for example, by keeping high __________ on the exports of developing countries.
options: trade barriers (tariffs and subsidies protecting their own farmers/industries)
solution: As a member of the WTO, India (and other developing countries) has argued that the developed countries have not fully honoured their commitments to free and fair trade, and that the global trade rules are tilted against the developing countries. In particular, the developed countries are accused of: keeping high trade barriers (tariffs and non-tariff barriers) against the exports (especially agricultural and labour-intensive goods) of developing countries; and giving huge subsidies to their own farmers and industries (which lets them export cheaply and undercut developing-country producers, while shielding their own markets). So developing countries feel that they have opened up their markets while the developed countries have not reciprocated fairly — a major grievance and criticism regarding the WTO/globalisation. Understanding this criticism of the WTO (unfair barriers/subsidies by developed countries) is a prelims-relevant point. India argues that developed countries keep high trade barriers and subsidies protecting their own producers, while pressing developing countries to open up.

stem: The reforms also relaxed the restrictions of the MRTP Act (which had limited the growth of big companies). This reflected the reforms' aim to:
options: free big businesses to grow and expand (removing limits on their size/expansion)
solution: The reforms relaxed (and later replaced) the restrictions of the MRTP Act (the Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices Act) — which had earlier put limits on the growth and expansion of big companies/business houses (to prevent the concentration of economic power and monopolies). Relaxing these restrictions reflected the reforms' aim to free big businesses to grow and expand according to market opportunities (removing the earlier limits on their size and expansion), as part of the general liberalisation and the reduced role of controls. (The MRTP Act was later replaced by the Competition Act, which focuses on promoting competition rather than merely restricting size.) Understanding the relaxation of MRTP restrictions is a prelims point. The reforms relaxed the MRTP Act's restrictions, freeing big businesses to grow and expand.

stem: The freeing of imports and reduction of tariffs benefited Indian __________, who got access to a wider variety of (and often cheaper) goods.
solution: The freeing of imports and the reduction of tariffs (as part of globalisation) benefited Indian consumers, who gained access to a much wider variety of goods (including foreign brands and products that were earlier unavailable or restricted), often of better quality and at lower/competitive prices (due to the competition from imports and the entry of foreign/multinational companies). So, after the reforms, Indian consumers enjoyed far more choice and better access to goods and services (from cars and electronics to many consumer products) than in the earlier era of a closed, controlled economy. This benefit to consumers is one of the positive aspects of liberalisation/globalisation. Understanding this consumer benefit is a prelims point. Freeing imports and lowering tariffs benefited Indian consumers, giving them a wider variety of (often cheaper) goods.

stem: A criticism regarding the pattern of post-reform growth is that the industrial/manufacturing sector's growth (and its share) did NOT rise as much as hoped, which is a problem because manufacturing is important for:
options: creating large-scale employment (jobs) for the workforce
solution: A criticism regarding the pattern of India's post-reform growth is that the industrial/manufacturing sector's growth (and its share in the economy) did not rise as much as had been hoped (the growth being led instead by services). This is a problem/concern because the manufacturing sector is especially important for creating large-scale employment — manufacturing (industry) can absorb large numbers of workers (including less-skilled workers moving out of agriculture), which is exactly what a country like India, with a huge and growing labour force, needs. Because manufacturing lagged, it did not generate enough jobs — contributing to the problem of 'jobless growth' and the persistence of unemployment/underemployment. So the sluggish manufacturing is a key concern in the appraisal. Understanding why lagging manufacturing is a problem (jobs) is a prelims point. Lagging manufacturing growth is a concern because manufacturing is important for creating the large-scale employment that India needs.

stem: The reforms are said to have benefited some sections and regions more than others; broadly, the __________ areas and the more skilled/educated gained more.
solution: The reforms are said to have benefited some sections and regions more than others (an uneven distribution of gains). Broadly, the urban areas (cities), and the more skilled, educated, and better-off people (and the more developed states/regions), gained more from the reforms and the faster growth — because the growth was concentrated in the urban-based, skill-intensive service and industrial sectors, which favoured those with education, skills, and access to opportunities. Meanwhile, the rural areas, the agricultural sector, the less-skilled, and the backward regions benefited less (or were even adversely affected). This uneven pattern is why the reforms are criticised for increasing inequality/disparities. Understanding that urban/skilled sections gained more is a prelims point. The reforms broadly benefited the urban areas and the more skilled/educated more than the rural areas and the less-skilled.

stem: The pre-1991 policy of 'import substitution' was replaced, under the reforms, by a more __________ (open) trade policy.
solution: The pre-1991 policy of import substitution (the inward-looking strategy of replacing imports with domestically-produced goods, behind high protective barriers) was replaced, under the reforms, by a more outward-looking, open trade policy — one that reduced trade barriers (tariffs and restrictions), opened the economy up to foreign trade and competition, and encouraged exports and integration with the world economy (globalisation). So India shifted from an inward-looking, protectionist stance to an outward-looking, more open and globally-integrated stance in its trade policy. Understanding this shift (import substitution → open, outward-looking policy) is a prelims point. The reforms replaced the inward-looking import-substitution policy with a more outward-looking, open trade policy.

stem: 'Navratnas' were a set of important, well-performing __________ that were given greater autonomy (managerial and financial freedom) to become globally competitive.
solution: 'Navratnas' (meaning 'nine jewels') were a select group of important, large, and well-performing public-sector enterprises (PSEs) that the government granted greater autonomy — that is, greater managerial and financial freedom/powers to take their own decisions (on investment, expansion, etc.) — so that they could improve their efficiency and performance and become globally competitive (and expand, even internationally). This policy (of identifying and empowering the best PSEs as Navratnas, and similarly 'Maharatnas' and 'Miniratnas') reflected the effort to make the public sector more efficient and competitive (rather than simply privatising everything). Understanding the 'Navratna' PSEs (given greater autonomy) is a prelims-relevant point. 'Navratnas' were well-performing public-sector enterprises given greater autonomy to become globally competitive.

stem: The abolition of the License Raj benefited entrepreneurship by:
options: making it harder to start businesses
making it easier and quicker to start and run businesses (freeing entrepreneurs from red tape and permits)
solution: The abolition of the License Raj (the dismantling of the elaborate system of industrial licences, permits, and controls) benefited entrepreneurship by making it much easier and quicker to start and run businesses. With licensing abolished for most industries, entrepreneurs no longer had to obtain government permission (and endure the red tape, delays, and corruption) to set up, expand, or diversify an industry — they were free to make their own business decisions and respond to market opportunities. This unleashed entrepreneurial energy and enterprise, encouraging new businesses and investment. So the end of the License Raj was a boost to entrepreneurship and private enterprise. Understanding this benefit of ending the License Raj is a prelims point. Abolishing the License Raj made it easier and quicker to start and run businesses, boosting entrepreneurship.

stem: The convertibility of the rupee on the 'current account' (introduced in the reforms) means the rupee can be freely exchanged for foreign currency for the purpose of:
options: trade (imports and exports) and other current transactions (like travel, remittances)
solution: Current-account convertibility of the rupee (introduced in the mid-1990s as part of the reforms) means that the rupee can be freely exchanged for foreign currency (at market-determined rates) for the purposes of current-account transactions — that is, for trade (paying for imports and receiving payment for exports), and for other current transactions like foreign travel, education, medical expenses, and remittances (sending/receiving money). This made trade and current dealings much easier and freer (part of opening up/globalisation). (Note: full 'capital-account' convertibility — free exchange for investment/capital purposes like buying foreign assets — was not fully allowed, being kept restricted for stability.) Understanding current-account convertibility is a prelims-relevant point. Current-account convertibility lets the rupee be freely exchanged for foreign currency for trade and other current transactions.

stem: A social/cultural concern about globalisation is that it may lead to:
options: the erosion of local cultures and traditions (and the dominance of a homogenised, Western/global consumer culture)
solution: A social/cultural concern about globalisation is that it may lead to the erosion (weakening/loss) of local cultures, traditions, and identities, and the spread of a homogenised (uniform), often Western-influenced, global consumer culture. As global media, brands, products, films, food, and lifestyles spread across the world, critics worry that they may overwhelm and displace diverse local cultures, languages, customs, and ways of life — making cultures everywhere more similar (and more commercialised/consumerist), at the cost of cultural diversity and local identity. So, alongside its economic effects, globalisation raises this cultural concern. Understanding the cultural concern about globalisation is a prelims-relevant point. A cultural concern about globalisation is the erosion of local cultures and the spread of a homogenised, Western/global consumer culture.

stem: Special Economic Zones (SEZs) were set up as part of the reforms to promote exports; they are areas that have:
options: special (favourable) economic rules — like tax concessions and fewer regulations — to attract investment and boost exports
solution: Special Economic Zones (SEZs) are specially-designated areas/regions that are given special, favourable economic rules and incentives — such as tax concessions/exemptions, relaxed regulations, and good infrastructure — that are more liberal than those prevailing in the rest of the country. They were set up (as part of the reforms/globalisation) to attract investment (both domestic and foreign) and to promote exports (and create jobs), by providing an attractive, hassle-free environment for export-oriented businesses. So SEZs are enclaves of liberalised policy aimed at boosting investment and exports. Understanding SEZs (special zones with favourable rules to boost investment/exports) is a prelims-relevant point. Special Economic Zones (SEZs) are areas with special favourable economic rules (tax concessions, fewer regulations) to attract investment and boost exports.

stem: The overall appraisal of the reforms is best described as:
options: a mixed/balanced verdict — with significant achievements (faster growth, stability, opening up) but also serious concerns (jobless growth, neglect of agriculture, inequality)
solution: The overall appraisal (assessment) of the 1991 reforms is best described as a mixed/balanced verdict — recognising both significant achievements and serious concerns. On the positive side: the reforms raised India's economic growth rate, ended the balance-of-payments crisis and built up large foreign-exchange reserves, opened up and modernised the economy, boosted the service/IT sector and exports, attracted foreign investment, and gave consumers more choice. On the negative side: the reforms are criticised for 'jobless growth' (not enough employment), the neglect of agriculture (slow farm growth, reduced public investment), rising inequality (widening gaps between rich and poor and between regions), the pressure on small producers and the poor, and the lagging of manufacturing. So the balanced appraisal is that the reforms brought real gains but also real costs/shortcomings — a mixed outcome. Understanding this balanced appraisal is the key takeaway of the chapter. The appraisal of the reforms is a mixed verdict — real achievements (growth, stability, opening up) alongside serious concerns (jobless growth, agricultural neglect, inequality).

stem: Assertion (A): India opened up its economy to foreign competition after 1991. Reason (R): It was believed that competition would force Indian producers to become more efficient and improve the quality of their goods. Which is correct?
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
solution: Both the Assertion and the Reason are true, and the Reason correctly explains the Assertion. It is true (A) that India opened up its economy to foreign competition after 1991 (by reducing tariffs and import restrictions and allowing foreign goods and companies in). And the reason is (R) that it was believed (a key rationale for this opening up) that exposing Indian producers to competition — from imports and foreign firms — would force them to become more efficient (cut costs, modernise) and to improve the quality of their products, in order to survive and compete (whereas the earlier protection had made them inefficient and complacent). So the belief that competition would spur efficiency and quality (R) is exactly why the economy was opened to foreign competition (A). Understanding this rationale for opening up is a prelims point. India opened its economy to foreign competition believing that competition would force its producers to become more efficient and improve quality.

stem: The reforms marked a shift in India's development strategy from a state-led, controlled economy toward a more __________ economy.
solution: The reforms of 1991 marked a fundamental shift in India's development strategy — from the earlier model of a state-led, controlled, and inward-looking economy (with heavy government controls, a dominant public sector, and protectionism) toward a more market-oriented (market-led), open economy — in which market forces, private enterprise, competition, and integration with the world economy play a much bigger role, and the government's role is reduced to more of a regulator/facilitator. This shift from 'state to market' (and from a closed to an open economy) is the essence of what the reforms changed. Understanding this basic shift (state-led → market-oriented) is a key prelims point. The reforms shifted India's strategy from a state-led, controlled economy toward a more market-oriented, open economy.

stem: The set of conditions/reforms that the IMF and World Bank required borrowing countries (like India in 1991) to adopt is called a __________ programme.
solution: The set of conditions and reforms that the IMF and World Bank required borrowing countries (like India in 1991) to adopt, in return for their loans, is called a 'Structural Adjustment Programme' (SAP). These programmes typically require the borrowing country to undertake economic reforms — such as liberalising the economy, reducing government controls and the fiscal deficit, privatising, devaluing the currency, and opening up to trade and foreign investment — in order to correct its economic imbalances and 'adjust' the structure of its economy. India's 1991 reforms were undertaken partly under such a structural adjustment programme (as a condition of its IMF/World Bank loans). Understanding the term 'structural adjustment programme' is a prelims-relevant point. A 'Structural Adjustment Programme' is the set of reforms the IMF/World Bank require borrowing countries to adopt (as India did in 1991).

stem: The immediate origin of the 1991 economic crisis lay in a severe __________ crisis, in which India could barely finance its imports.
solution: By 1991 India faced an acute balance-of-payments crisis; foreign-exchange reserves had dropped so low that they could pay for only about two weeks of imports.

stem: A major underlying cause of the 1991 crisis was that the government had been spending far more than its income, leading to large and persistent:
solution: Years of heavy government spending (on inefficient public enterprises, subsidies, etc.) beyond revenue produced mounting fiscal deficits, borrowing and debt, culminating in the 1991 crisis.

stem: During the 1991 crisis, India's foreign-exchange reserves had fallen to a level sufficient to pay for imports of only about:
solution: Reserves had dropped to around US$1 billion — enough to cover only about two weeks of imports — forcing India to approach the IMF/World Bank.

stem: To secure emergency loans from the IMF and World Bank in 1991, India had to agree to:
options: liberalise and restructure its economy (a set of conditions/reforms)
solution: The IMF and World Bank gave loans on the condition that India open up and restructure (liberalise) its economy — the structural adjustment programme.

stem: The set of conditions/reforms that the IMF and World Bank required India to adopt in 1991 is known as a __________ programme.
solution: The reforms undertaken as a condition for IMF/World Bank loans are collectively called the Structural Adjustment Programme (also New Economic Policy).

stem: The 1991 reform measures are of two broad kinds: short-run 'stabilisation measures' to correct the immediate crisis, and long-run '__________ reforms' to improve efficiency.
solution: Stabilisation measures addressed the balance-of-payments and inflation problems in the short run; structural reform measures aimed to improve the economy's efficiency and competitiveness over the long run.

stem: As part of the 1991 reforms, the Indian rupee was __________, reducing its external value to make exports more competitive.
solution: The rupee was devalued in 1991 to make Indian exports cheaper and imports dearer, helping to correct the balance-of-payments deficit.

stem: The Finance Minister who introduced the 1991 reforms (under PM P.V. Narasimha Rao) was:
solution: Dr. Manmohan Singh, as Finance Minister in the Narasimha Rao government, spearheaded the 1991 economic reforms.

stem: 'Liberalisation' of the economy in 1991 meant the removal of unnecessary controls and restrictions, such as ending:
solution: Liberalisation freed the economy from controls — abolishing industrial licensing for most industries, freeing prices, and easing rules on trade, investment and finance.

stem: After the 1991 reforms, industrial licensing was abolished for almost all industries EXCEPT a few (like alcohol, cigarettes, defence equipment, and hazardous chemicals). The number of industries reserved for the public sector was reduced to just:
solution: The number of industries reserved exclusively for the public sector was cut sharply from 17 to only a handful (3, later 2 — atomic energy and railways).

stem: 'Privatisation' refers to the transfer of ownership, management or control of __________ enterprises to the private sector.
solution: Privatisation means shedding government ownership/management of public-sector enterprises, often by selling shares to the private sector or the public.

stem: The sale of a part of the equity (shares) of a public-sector enterprise to the private sector or the public is called:
solution: Disinvestment is the sale of a portion of the government's shareholding in a public-sector enterprise, a key tool of privatisation.

stem: Well-performing, important public-sector enterprises were given greater managerial and financial autonomy to make them globally competitive; these were called:
solution: Selected profitable PSEs were granted greater autonomy as 'Navratnas', 'Miniratnas' and later 'Maharatnas' to help them compete globally.

stem: 'Globalisation' refers to the integration of a country's economy with the __________ economy.
solution: Globalisation is the process of integrating the national economy with the world economy through freer flows of trade, capital, technology and (to some extent) labour.

stem: 'Outsourcing' is a feature of globalisation in which a company:
options: hires regular external/foreign agencies to do some of its services (like call centres, IT)
solution: Outsourcing means getting services (such as IT support, BPO, call centres, accounting) done by external agencies, often abroad, to save costs — a major source of jobs in India.

stem: India became a favoured destination for outsourcing chiefly because of its:
options: large pool of skilled, English-speaking workers available at relatively low wages
solution: India's abundant, skilled, English-speaking and comparatively low-cost workforce, along with improving IT infrastructure, made it a leading destination for outsourcing.

stem: The World Trade Organisation (WTO), which India joined, was established in which year to oversee the rules of international trade?
solution: The WTO was set up in 1995 (succeeding GATT) to establish and enforce rules for liberalised international trade among member countries.

stem: India, as a developing country in the WTO, has criticised developed countries for:
options: not fully honouring their commitments and keeping high tariffs/trade barriers against exports from developing countries
solution: India and other developing nations argue that developed countries have retained high tariffs and non-tariff barriers on developing-country exports and have not fully opened their own markets.

stem: Investment by foreign companies in the businesses of another country (setting up or acquiring firms) is called:
solution: Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) is investment by foreign firms/individuals in the enterprises of another country; the reforms eased restrictions on FDI.

stem: Foreign investors like foreign banks and mutual funds that were allowed to invest in India's financial markets after the reforms are called:
solution: Foreign Institutional Investors (FIIs) — such as foreign merchant banks, mutual funds and pension funds — were permitted to invest in India's stock and financial markets.

stem: As part of tax reforms, the rates of DIRECT taxes (like income tax and corporate tax) were generally:
options: reduced (moderated) to encourage compliance and investment
solution: Tax reforms lowered the very high rates of direct taxes, on the view that moderate rates encourage saving, investment and better tax compliance.

stem: The unified indirect tax introduced in India in 2017, replacing many separate indirect taxes, is the:
solution: The Goods and Services Tax (GST), introduced in 2017, replaced a host of central and state indirect taxes with a single unified indirect tax.

stem: Under the reforms, the Reserve Bank of India's role changed from that of a __________ of the financial sector to a facilitator/regulator.
solution: Financial-sector reforms shifted the RBI from a direct 'controller' to a 'regulator/facilitator', allowing market forces and private/foreign banks a greater role.

stem: 'Current account convertibility' of the rupee (introduced in the reforms) means the rupee can be freely converted into foreign currency for:
options: trade in goods and services and other current transactions
solution: Current-account convertibility allows free conversion of the rupee for trade in goods and services and current transactions (like travel, remittances), though capital-account convertibility remains regulated.

stem: A striking feature of India's post-1991 growth is that it has been led mainly by the __________ sector.
solution: Post-reform growth has been driven chiefly by the service sector — especially IT, software, telecom, finance and business services — rather than manufacturing.

stem: A major criticism of the reforms is that the fast growth was 'jobless growth', meaning that:
options: growth was not accompanied by a proportionate increase in employment
solution: Critics point to 'jobless growth' — GDP grew rapidly but employment did not grow in proportion, so unemployment remained a serious problem.

stem: Another criticism of the reforms is that they NEGLECTED the __________ sector, where public investment and growth slowed.
solution: Agriculture was relatively neglected after the reforms — reduced public investment, removal of subsidies and exposure to global competition slowed its growth, hurting the majority who depend on it.

stem: A further criticism is that the reforms increased __________ — widening the gap between rich and poor and between developed and backward regions.
solution: The reforms are criticised for widening income and regional inequalities, as the benefits went disproportionately to skilled workers, urban areas and richer states.

stem: A concern about globalisation for small domestic producers is that they:
options: may be unable to compete with large multinational corporations and cheaper imports
solution: Small domestic producers may be outcompeted by large multinationals and cheap imports, threatening their survival — a common criticism of globalisation.

stem: The manufacturing/industrial sector's growth after the reforms did NOT rise as much as hoped, which is a concern because manufacturing is important for:
options: creating large-scale employment and absorbing surplus labour from agriculture
solution: Slow manufacturing growth is worrying because manufacturing generates mass employment; its weakness means fewer jobs for workers moving out of agriculture.

stem: Special Economic Zones (SEZs) were set up to promote exports; they are areas that enjoy:
options: special economic laws, tax concessions and simplified rules to attract investment and boost exports
solution: SEZs are duty-free enclaves with liberal economic laws, tax incentives and simplified procedures, meant to attract investment and promote exports.

stem: The relaxation of the MRTP Act (Monopolies and Restrictive Trade Practices) under the reforms reflected the aim to:
options: allow big companies to expand and no longer require prior approval for expansion
solution: Liberalisation eased the MRTP restrictions so that large companies could expand and diversify without needing prior government approval, encouraging growth.

stem: The abolition of the 'Licence Raj' benefited entrepreneurship by:
options: freeing entrepreneurs to start and expand businesses without needing government permits, unleashing enterprise
solution: Ending industrial licensing removed a major barrier, allowing entrepreneurs to set up and expand businesses freely, spurring private enterprise and competition.

stem: The freeing of imports and reduction of tariffs benefited Indian __________, who gained access to a wider variety of, and often cheaper, goods.
solution: Lower tariffs and freer imports gave consumers access to a wider range of, and often cheaper and better-quality, goods.

stem: The body that replaced the Planning Commission in 2015, reflecting a shift from a directive to an advisory role, is:
solution: The NITI Aayog (National Institution for Transforming India) replaced the Planning Commission in 2015, acting as a policy think-tank/advisory body rather than a directive planning authority.

stem: The increase in foreign-exchange reserves after the reforms had the effect of:
options: overcoming the balance-of-payments problem and giving the economy stability and confidence
solution: Rising foreign-exchange reserves resolved the balance-of-payments crisis and gave the economy stability and the confidence of foreign investors.

stem: Which of the following is TRUE about the impact of reforms on the agricultural sector?
options: Agricultural growth decelerated due to reduced public investment, removal of subsidies and exposure to global price fluctuations
solution: Post-reform, agriculture's growth slowed because of cuts in public investment, reduction of subsidies, and exposure to volatile global prices, even as most Indians still depend on it.

stem: The pre-1991 policy of import substitution was replaced under the reforms by a more __________ trade policy.
solution: The reforms replaced inward-looking import substitution with a more open, outward-looking, trade policy that reduced protection and encouraged trade and competition.

stem: Which of the following best explains why competition (from opening up) was expected to benefit consumers?
options: It forces producers to become more efficient and improve quality and lower prices
solution: Opening the economy to competition pressures domestic producers to become more efficient, improve quality and cut prices — benefiting consumers.

stem: The reforms allowed foreign technology and investment into India, which helped to:
options: modernise production, raise productivity and improve the quality of goods
solution: Access to foreign technology and capital helped modernise Indian industry, raise productivity and improve product quality and competitiveness.

stem: An overall balanced appraisal of the 1991 reforms is that they:
options: raised growth and integrated India with the world, but were criticised for jobless growth, neglect of agriculture, and rising inequality
solution: The reforms boosted growth, foreign investment and the service sector and ended the crisis, but critics point to jobless growth, agricultural neglect and increased inequality — a mixed record.

stem: The 1991 reforms marked a fundamental shift in India's development strategy from a state-led, controlled economy toward a more __________ economy.
solution: The reforms shifted India from a heavily controlled, state-led model to a more market-oriented, open and competitive economy.

stem: The reduction of quantitative restrictions (like quotas) and licences on imports was part of which reform component?
solution: Removing quantitative restrictions and import licences and lowering tariffs were part of the globalisation/trade-liberalisation measures that opened India to world trade.

stem: The growth of the IT and software services industry made India a major __________ of software and IT-enabled services.
solution: India became a leading exporter of software and IT-enabled/business-process services, a hallmark of its post-reform, service-led growth.

stem: Which statement about the OVERALL message of the LPG chapter is most accurate?
options: The reforms accelerated growth and modernised the economy, but their benefits were uneven, so growth must be made more inclusive and job-creating
solution: The chapter concludes that the LPG reforms revived and accelerated growth and integrated India globally, but that the gains were unevenly shared, so the challenge is to make growth more inclusive, employment-generating and balanced.

stem: Under the reforms, the rupee's exchange rate was increasingly determined by:
options: market forces of demand and supply (a managed/floating rate)
solution: After the reforms, the rupee moved toward a market-determined (managed float) exchange rate, set largely by demand and supply in the foreign-exchange market.

stem: The removal of the requirement for prior government approval to import capital goods and raw materials was intended to:
options: make it easier for firms to modernise and expand production
solution: Freeing imports of capital goods and raw materials from licensing let firms access technology and inputs more easily, helping them modernise and expand.

stem: The overall message of the chapter 'Liberalisation, Privatisation and Globalisation: An Appraisal' is that:
options: In 1991, facing a severe economic crisis, India launched major reforms — Liberalisation, Privatisation, and Globalisation (LPG) — that opened up and freed the economy, raising its growth rate, foreign reserves, and the service sector; but these reforms are appraised as a mixed outcome, since they also brought serious concerns like jobless growth, the neglect of agriculture, and rising inequality
The reforms ended the Indian economy
solution: The chapter conveys that in 1991, facing a severe economic crisis (especially a balance-of-payments/foreign-exchange crisis, with reserves almost exhausted, a large fiscal deficit, and high inflation), India launched a major set of economic reforms — the New Economic Policy of Liberalisation, Privatisation, and Globalisation (LPG). Liberalisation freed the economy from many controls (abolishing industrial licensing — the 'License Raj', easing regulations, and reforming the financial, tax, and trade systems); Privatisation reduced the role of the public sector and expanded that of the private sector (through disinvestment and by opening up reserved sectors); and Globalisation integrated India with the world economy (reducing tariffs and restrictions, encouraging foreign trade and foreign investment/FDI, and joining the WTO). The chapter then offers an 'appraisal' (a balanced assessment) of these reforms — showing that they had significant positive effects (a higher rate of GDP growth, a large build-up of foreign-exchange reserves that ended the crisis, a boom in the service/IT sector, more foreign investment, and a greater availability of goods), but also serious shortcomings and criticisms ('jobless growth' — growth without enough employment; the neglect of agriculture, which grew slowly with reduced public investment; rising inequality between the rich and poor and between regions; and concerns about the effects of globalisation on small producers and on the poor). So the reforms are appraised as a mixed outcome — a turning point that spurred growth and opened up the economy, but at the cost of neglecting some sectors and worsening some disparities. Understanding the reasons for, the components of, and the balanced appraisal (both gains and criticisms) of the 1991 reforms is the central concern of this chapter. Facing a 1991 crisis, India launched the LPG reforms, which opened up and accelerated the economy but are appraised as a mixed outcome — with gains in growth and reserves alongside concerns like jobless growth, agricultural neglect, and rising inequality.
